text: If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
reflection: Jesus asks a probing question about how we handle money: "If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?" Mammon means worldly wealth, the kind that comes and goes. Jesus is saying that our everyday faithfulness with ordinary things reveals whether we are ready for greater things. How we spend, save, give, and handle what is entrusted to us is not separate from our spiritual life. It is a training ground for it. Living by faith is not only about grand moments of trust. It shows up in paying bills honestly, giving generously, and refusing to let money become our master. The true riches Jesus speaks of are the treasures of His kingdom: deeper fellowship with God, spiritual responsibility, and eternal reward. Today, look at your finances as an act of faith. Ask God to make you faithful in small things, and trust Him to entrust you with what truly lasts.
question: How could the way you handle money and small things become an act of faith today?
prayer: Lord, everything I have is entrusted to me by You. Make me faithful with small and ordinary things, and teach me to value the true riches that last. Amen.

text: Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father…
reflection: Paul remembered the Thessalonians with gratitude, and he named three things that made their faith beautiful: "your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ." Notice how each virtue produces something. Faith works. Love labors. Hope endures with patience. These were not people who simply believed the right things. Their beliefs had hands and feet. Their faith moved them to action, their love moved them to sacrifice, and their hope kept them steady through persecution. Faith that never acts is like a seed that never grows. Love that never labors is only sentiment. Hope that gives up at the first trouble is only wishful thinking. But when all three are rooted in Jesus, they produce a life that others remember with thanks. Today, ask yourself how your faith is working, how your love is laboring, and how your hope is enduring. Then take one practical step that puts your faith into loving action.
question: How is your faith working, your love laboring, and your hope enduring today?
prayer: Lord, give my faith hands and feet. Let my faith work, my love labor, and my hope endure with patience, so my life brings You glory. Amen.

text: Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference…
reflection: Paul has spent the opening chapters of Romans showing that every one of us falls short. Then comes the good news: "Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference." No difference. That phrase cuts both ways. We are all equally in need of grace, and we are all equally welcome to receive it. There is no special class of people who can earn God's approval, and no group too far gone to be saved. The righteousness we could never achieve is offered to us as a gift through faith in Jesus. This levels every proud heart and lifts every discouraged one. You do not have to compare yourself with others to know where you stand with God. If you trust in Jesus, His righteousness covers you completely. Today, rest in that gift. And look at others with fresh eyes, remembering that there is no difference at the foot of the cross.
question: Whom do you need to see with fresh eyes, remembering there is no difference at the foot of the cross?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the righteousness that comes by faith in Jesus. I rest in Your gift, and I ask You to help me see every person as equally in need of Your grace. Amen.

text: But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.
reflection: This verse begins with a hard truth: "the scripture hath concluded all under sin." Like a prison door closing, God's Word shows that none of us can free ourselves by our own efforts. But the purpose of that hard truth is not despair. It is hope. Paul continues, "that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe." The bad news makes room for the good news. Only when we realize we cannot save ourselves do we become ready to receive a Savior. Many people spend their lives trying to prove they are good enough. They feel the constant pressure to earn approval from God and others. But faith lets you set down that impossible burden. The promise is given, not earned. It comes to those who believe. Today, if you feel trapped by your failures, hear this verse as an invitation. You do not need to break out on your own. Trust Jesus, and receive the promise He freely gives.
question: Which failure makes you feel trapped, and can you trust Jesus to set you free from it?
prayer: Lord, I cannot free myself by my own efforts. I trust in Jesus and receive the promise You freely give to those who believe. Amen.

text: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him.
reflection: James paints a tender picture of a church caring for its sick. The elders come, they pray, they anoint with oil, and James promises: "the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him." Notice that healing and forgiveness appear side by side. God cares about the whole person: body, heart, and soul. Sometimes we carry physical pain. Sometimes we carry the heavier weight of guilt. James assures us that God meets both needs with compassion. And He often does it through community. The sick person is not left to suffer alone; others come and pray. Is there someone in your life who is unwell or burdened today? Visit them, call them, or pray with them in faith. And if you are the one who is hurting, do not hide. Invite others to pray for you. The Lord who raises up is also the Lord who forgives.
question: Who is sick or burdened that you could visit, call, or pray with in faith today?
prayer: Lord, You care for the whole person, body, heart, and soul. Raise up the sick, forgive the burdened, and make me faithful to pray for those who are hurting. Amen.

text: But Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.
reflection: The writer of Hebrews compares Moses, a faithful servant in God's house, with Jesus, the Son who rules over it. Then comes a surprising line: "whose house are we." We are God's house, the very place where He lives among His people. What a privilege. And the verse continues with a call: "if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end." Our confidence is not in ourselves. It is in the character of Christ, the faithful Son who never fails. Because He is trustworthy, we can hold on with boldness and even joy. Some seasons test that confidence. Doubts whisper, troubles mount, and hope feels thin. That is when we remember who holds the house together. It is not our strength but His faithfulness. Today, choose to hold fast. Rejoice in the hope you have, even if it feels small. The Son who rules over God's house will keep you to the end.
question: What hope, even a small one, can you choose to hold fast to today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Son over God's house, thank You for making me part of Your dwelling place. Help me hold fast to my hope, trusting Your faithfulness to keep me to the end. Amen.

text: Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator.
reflection: Peter wrote to believers who were suffering for their faith. He did not promise them that the pain would end quickly. Instead, he gave them a way to walk through it: "let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator." To commit something is to hand it over for safekeeping, like depositing a treasure with someone you trust. Peter invites us to entrust our very souls to God. And he reminds us of who God is: a faithful Creator. The One who made you knows how to keep you. He has not lost control of the world He formed. Meanwhile, we keep doing good. Suffering does not have to make us bitter or idle. It can become an opportunity to trust more deeply and love more faithfully. If you are suffering today, hand your soul to God again. Keep doing what is right, and rest in His faithful care.
question: What suffering can you hand over to your faithful Creator today while you keep doing good?
prayer: Faithful Creator, I commit the keeping of my soul to You. Help me keep doing what is right while I suffer, and let me rest in Your faithful care. Amen.

text: In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge.
reflection: Many people chase confidence through achievement, appearance, or approval. But Proverbs offers a different source: "In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge." The fear of the Lord is not terror. It is a deep reverence that puts God in His rightful place. When we honor Him above everything else, we stop being ruled by lesser fears: the fear of failure, of rejection, of what others think. Our confidence becomes strong because it rests on Someone who cannot be shaken. And there is a beautiful promise for families here. Those who walk in reverence for God provide a place of refuge for their children. A home built on trust in God becomes a shelter in life's storms. Today, let reverence for God steady your heart. Turn from anxious striving and rest in His strength. And pray for the next generation, that they too would find a safe refuge in Him.
question: Which lesser fear, failure, rejection, or others' opinions, is ruling you that reverence for God could quiet?
prayer: Lord, let my confidence rest in You, not in achievement or approval. Be my place of refuge, and be a refuge for the generation that comes after me. Amen.

text: And having this confidence, I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith…
reflection: Paul was in prison, unsure whether he would live or die. Yet he wrote with settled confidence: "I know that I shall abide and continue with you all for your furtherance and joy of faith." He believed God still had work for him to do, and that work was helping others grow and rejoice in their faith. What a beautiful purpose for any life. Paul did not see his days as his own. He saw them as gifts to be spent for the good of others. Whatever time God gave him, he wanted to use it to help people flourish. Your life also has purpose. Whether you are young or old, healthy or struggling, God has placed people around you whose faith and joy you can encourage. You do not have to be a preacher. A kind word, a shared verse, a listening ear, or a faithful example can help someone take another step forward. Today, ask God whose faith and joy you can help increase.
question: Whose faith and joy could you help grow today with a kind word or a faithful example?
prayer: Lord, my days are Your gift. Use them for the good of others, and show me whose faith and joy I can help increase today. Amen.

text: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
reflection: Paul gives Timothy a simple but powerful plan for passing on the faith: "the things that thou hast heard of me … the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also." Count the generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others beyond them. The gospel moves forward like a relay race, each runner receiving the baton and handing it to the next. None of us came to faith on our own. Someone taught us, prayed for us, or showed us Jesus. And now we have the privilege of passing it on. Notice the qualities Paul looks for: faithful and able to teach. A teachable heart comes first. Those who keep learning become the ones who can help others learn. Today, thank God for those who handed the faith to you. Then ask yourself who you are passing it to. A child, a friend, a coworker. Faith grows strongest when it is shared.
question: Who handed the faith to you, and to whom are you passing it on?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the faithful people who taught me about You. Make me faithful to pass on what I have received to someone who will teach others also. Amen.

text: For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth.
reflection: This psalm was written by someone who had walked with God for a long time. Looking back over many years, the psalmist prays, "For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth." There is a quiet strength in that kind of faith. It is not based on one exciting experience but on a lifetime of God's faithfulness. Through joys and sorrows, victories and failures, God proved Himself trustworthy again and again. If you have known God for many years, take time today to remember. Recall the prayers He answered, the storms He carried you through, the times He provided when you did not know how. Let those memories strengthen your trust for what lies ahead. And if you are young in faith, take heart. You are beginning a story that God will be faithful to write. One day you too will look back and say that He has been your hope all along.
question: Looking back, where has God been your hope and trust all along?
prayer: Lord God, You have been my hope and my trust from my youth. Thank You for a lifetime of faithfulness, and help me trust You for all that lies ahead. Amen.

text: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him.
reflection: Imagine being invited into the throne room of a king. Most people would hesitate, unsure of their welcome. But Paul says that in Christ we have "boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him." Through Jesus, the door to God's presence is open, and we are welcome to come in, not timidly, but boldly. This boldness is not arrogance. It does not come from our own goodness. It comes from trusting Jesus, who has made the way for us. Because of Him, you never have to wonder whether God wants to hear from you. You never have to clean yourself up before you pray. You can come to Him in the morning with your plans, at midday with your stress, and at night with your tears. He is always available, always attentive. Today, take Him at His word. Come to God boldly in prayer. Bring your requests, your thanks, and your heart. Through faith in Christ, you are always welcome.
question: What request or thanks can you bring boldly to God in prayer today?
prayer: Lord, through faith in Jesus I have boldness and access to You. I come today with my requests, my thanks, and my heart, knowing I am always welcome. Amen.

text: Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
reflection: In the famous chapter on love, Paul describes four things that love does: "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things." Love bears, quietly carrying burdens and covering faults instead of exposing them. Love believes, choosing to think the best rather than the worst. Love hopes, refusing to give up on people or situations. And love endures, staying faithful through long seasons of difficulty. This is not naive optimism. It is faith in action. It trusts that God is still at work, even in people who seem stuck and situations that seem hopeless. Love like this is only possible because God first loved us this way. He bears with us, believes in His purposes for us, hopes for our good, and endures our wandering hearts. Today, think of someone you are tempted to give up on. Ask God to help you keep bearing, believing, hoping, and enduring. Faith-filled love can see what God is still able to do.
question: Whom are you tempted to give up on, and how can love keep bearing, believing, hoping, and enduring?
prayer: Lord, You have never given up on me. Teach me a love that bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things. Amen.

text: We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak…
reflection: Paul quotes a psalm to explain why he kept preaching despite hardship: "I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak." Faith does not stay silent. When something is truly believed, it naturally finds expression. Paul had every reason to stop talking about Jesus. He was persecuted, misunderstood, and worn out. But his faith compelled him to keep sharing the good news. The same spirit of faith lives in every believer. You do not need to be bold or eloquent. Speaking your faith can be as simple as telling a friend how God helped you this week, offering to pray with someone, or sharing why you have hope. What we believe shapes what we say. When our hearts are full of trust in God, our words begin to carry life to others. Today, let your faith find a voice. Speak a word of hope, encouragement, or testimony. Someone may need to hear exactly what you believe.
question: What word of hope or testimony could your faith speak to someone today?
prayer: Lord, I believe, and therefore I want to speak. Give my faith a voice today, and let my words carry hope and life to someone who needs it. Amen.

text: And Rabshakeh said unto them, Say ye now to Hezekiah, Thus saith the great king, the king of Assyria, What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?
reflection: The Assyrian army had surrounded Jerusalem, and their spokesman, Rabshakeh, delivered a taunting message to King Hezekiah: "What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?" It was meant to shake the people's faith. Everything around them looked hopeless. The enemy was mighty, and help seemed far away. Yet Hezekiah did not answer with panic. He took the threat to the temple and spread it before the Lord in prayer. And God delivered Jerusalem in a way no one expected. Sometimes we hear the same mocking question, whether from circumstances, other people, or our own doubts. Why do you still trust God? What good will it do? These moments test the foundation of our faith. But our confidence is not in our strength or in favorable circumstances. It is in the character of God, who has proven faithful again and again. Today, when doubts taunt you, do what Hezekiah did. Take them straight to God. His faithfulness is the answer to every taunt.
question: What doubt is taunting you, and how can you spread it out before the Lord as Hezekiah did?
prayer: Lord, when doubts ask what my confidence is, let me answer with Your faithfulness. I bring every threat and fear to You, trusting You to deliver me. Amen.

text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
reflection: This verse explains why faith matters so much: "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him." Faith begins with believing that God exists. But it does not stop there. It also trusts that He is good, that He responds to those who seek Him. Faith is not a leap into darkness. It is coming toward Someone, confident that He welcomes us. And notice the promise: God rewards those who diligently seek Him. The reward is not always wealth or ease. Most of all, the reward is God Himself, His presence, His peace, and His friendship. When you seek Him in prayer, in His Word, and in obedience, you are never wasting your time. He sees every step toward Him. Today, seek God with diligence. Come to Him believing that He is there and that He is good. Faith like that delights His heart.
question: How can you diligently seek God today, believing that He is there and that He is good?
prayer: Lord, I believe that You are, and that You reward those who diligently seek You. Draw me near in faith today, and let my trust delight Your heart. Amen.

text: For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?
reflection: Paul raises a question that many people ask: "For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?" In other words, if people are unfaithful, does that make God unfaithful? Paul's answer, in the next verse, is a resounding no. God's faithfulness does not depend on ours. His promises stand even when people fail to trust them. This is wonderful news. There are days when our faith feels weak. There are seasons when people around us, even people we love, turn away from God. It can make us wonder whether His promises still hold. But God remains exactly who He has always been. He keeps His word. Our wavering does not shake His steadiness. Today, if your faith feels fragile, lean on His faithfulness rather than your own. And if you are praying for someone who does not yet believe, keep praying. Their unbelief has not canceled God's love or His power.
question: Where does your faith feel fragile, and how can you lean on God's faithfulness instead?
prayer: Lord, Your faithfulness does not depend on mine. When my faith feels weak, hold me fast, and keep me praying for those who do not yet believe. Amen.

text: Though I might also have confidence in the flesh. If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more…
reflection: Paul had an impressive résumé. He came from the right family, trained under the right teachers, and kept the religious law with intense devotion. He wrote, "If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more." If anyone could have trusted in their own achievements, it was Paul. Yet in the verses that follow, he calls all of it loss compared to knowing Christ. His confidence moved from his own record to the character of Jesus. We all have things we are tempted to lean on: our accomplishments, reputation, morality, or religious activity. None of these are bad in themselves, but none can carry the weight of our souls. Only Christ can. There is great freedom in letting go of self-confidence and resting in Christ-confidence. You no longer have to prove yourself. Today, set down your résumé before God. Place your trust fully in Jesus, whose faithfulness is the only foundation that will never crumble.
question: What achievement or record are you still trusting in instead of Christ?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I set down my résumé before You. My confidence is not in my own record but in Your faithfulness, the foundation that will never crumble. Amen.

text: Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: When Paul summarized his years of ministry in Ephesus, he described his message in just a few words: "repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ." He shared this message with everyone, Jews and Greeks alike, without exception. Repentance and faith are two sides of the same turning. Repentance means turning away from sin and self-rule. Faith means turning toward Jesus with trust. You cannot fully do one without the other. And this turning is not a one-time event. It is the rhythm of the whole Christian life. Every day, we turn from what pulls us away and turn toward the One who loves us. That might sound heavy, but it is actually freeing. Repentance is not about shame; it is about coming home. Faith is not about striving; it is about trusting. Today, take a moment to turn again. Name anything that has drawn your heart away, and then lean your full trust on Jesus once more.
question: What has drawn your heart away that you can turn from, as you lean your trust on Jesus again?
prayer: Lord, I turn again toward You. Show me what has drawn my heart away, and help me turn from it and lean my full trust on Jesus. Amen.

text: To the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colosse: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: Paul's greeting to the Colossians is short, but it is full of identity and blessing: "To the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colosse: Grace be unto you, and peace." Notice what he calls them. Saints, meaning holy ones set apart for God. Faithful brethren, meaning trusting members of His family. These were ordinary people living in an ordinary town, yet God saw them as holy and faithful in Christ. Many of us do not feel like saints. We are aware of our flaws and failures. But our identity is not based on how we feel. It is based on being in Christ. In Him, you are set apart, loved, and part of a family. And to people like that, God gives grace and peace. Today, receive both. Let grace cover your shortcomings, and let peace settle your anxious thoughts. Live faithfully where you are, in your own ordinary town, as one of God's saints.
question: How might it change your day to see yourself as one of God's saints in your own ordinary place?
prayer: Father, thank You for calling me holy and faithful in Christ. Let Your grace cover my shortcomings and Your peace settle my anxious thoughts today. Amen.

text: But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation.
reflection: Paul describes believers as people who belong to the day, not the night. And people of the day get dressed for it: "putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation." A soldier would never go into battle without armor. In the same way, we face each day with spiritual protection. Faith and love guard our hearts, and hope guards our minds. Notice that love is part of the armor. We often think of protection as something hard and defensive, but Paul says love protects us too. It keeps our hearts from growing cold and bitter in a hurting world. Hope, meanwhile, protects our thoughts from despair. As we begin the week leading to Easter, remember that this armor was purchased for us by Christ. It is ours to put on every morning. Today, dress for the day. Choose faith over fear, love over bitterness, and hope over hopelessness.
question: Where do you need to choose faith over fear, love over bitterness, or hope over hopelessness today?
prayer: Lord, I belong to the day. Clothe me with the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation as I step into today. Amen.

text: Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ, to them that have obtained like precious faith with us through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ…
reflection: Peter opens his second letter with a remarkable statement. He writes to those "that have obtained like precious faith with us." Peter had walked with Jesus, seen the miracles, witnessed the resurrection, and preached at Pentecost. Yet he says that the faith of ordinary believers is just as precious as his own. There is no first-class or second-class faith in God's family. The faith you have is precious because of its object: Jesus Christ, our God and Savior. It was not earned; it was obtained, received as a gift through His righteousness. Perhaps you sometimes compare your faith with others and feel it is small or ordinary. Hear Peter's words for yourself. Your faith is precious. It connects you to the same Savior who called Peter by the sea. Treasure it. Nurture it through prayer and His Word. And never think that God values you less than the great names in history. In Christ, your faith shines just as brightly.
question: How can you treasure and nurture the precious faith God has given you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for the precious faith You have given me, as precious as any apostle's. Help me treasure it and nurture it through prayer and Your Word. Amen.

text: Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
reflection: David invites everyone, not just the strong or the spiritual, into a life of trust: "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us." At all times. Not only when life is easy, but in the middle of fear, grief, confusion, and pain. And how do we trust? By pouring out our hearts. God does not want polished prayers that hide our true feelings. He invites honesty. Pour it all out, the worry, the anger, the disappointment, the hope. Like water from a jar, empty everything before Him. He can handle it. He is a refuge, a safe place where we can be fully known and still fully loved. That is what makes Him trustworthy. Today, find a quiet moment and pour out your heart to God. Do not hold back. Tell Him what you are carrying. Then rest in the shelter of His presence. Selah: pause, and let that truth sink in.
question: What do you need to pour out honestly before God today?
prayer: Lord, You are my refuge at all times. I pour out my heart before You, the worry, the hurt, and the hope, and I rest in the shelter of Your presence. Amen.

text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
reflection: Paul ends his great chapter on love with a summary that has echoed through the centuries: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Faith, hope, and love all remain. They are the lasting virtues of the Christian life. But love is the greatest. Why? Because one day faith will become sight, and hope will be fulfilled. We will see God face to face and receive all He has promised. But love will continue forever. Love is the very nature of God, and it is the atmosphere of heaven. That means every act of love you show today has eternal value. Your patience with a child, your kindness to a stranger, your forgiveness of someone who hurt you, these are not small things. They are glimpses of eternity. This Holy Week, as we remember the greatest act of love in history, let love lead the way. Put faith and hope to work through love.
question: How can love lead the way for your faith and hope this week?
prayer: Lord, faith, hope, and love remain, but the greatest is love. As I remember Your great love this week, let love lead all I say and do. Amen.

text: Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
reflection: Proverbs uses two painful images to make a point: "Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint." Imagine trying to bite down on a broken tooth or walk on a dislocated foot. The very thing you are relying on gives way and makes the pain worse. That is what it is like to lean on someone unreliable when trouble comes. Most of us have experienced it. A promise not kept. Support that vanished when we needed it most. This proverb is not meant to make us cynical about people. It reminds us where ultimate trust belongs. Only God is perfectly faithful. He will never give way under the weight of our need. It also challenges us to become trustworthy ourselves. Today, place your deepest confidence in the Lord, who never fails. And ask Him to make you the kind of friend whom others can lean on in their time of trouble.
question: Where are you leaning on someone unreliable, and how can you become trustworthy for others?
prayer: Lord, You never fail. Let my deepest confidence rest in You, and make me the kind of friend others can lean on in their time of trouble. Amen.

text: My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust.
reflection: On this Good Friday, God's words through Isaiah carry special weight: "My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust." God's salvation is not far away. It has gone forth, reaching even to the distant islands, to the ends of the earth. And how did it go forth? Through the arms of Jesus stretched out on the cross. There, God's righteousness and salvation met. The arms that were nailed to the wood are the same arms that now hold all who trust in Him. Today, we remember the cost of our salvation. We remember the love that held nothing back. And we take comfort that this salvation is near, close enough to receive by faith. Whatever you are facing, rest in His arms. They are strong enough to save, and gentle enough to carry you home.
question: What are you facing today that you can bring into the arms stretched out for you on the cross?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Your arms stretched out on the cross brought salvation near. Thank You for Your sacrifice. Hold me in arms strong enough to save and gentle enough to carry me home. Amen.

text: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us…
reflection: The writer of Hebrews wants us to have a strong consolation, a deep and steady comfort. Where does it come from? From "two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie." God made a promise, and He confirmed it with an oath. Both are unchangeable, and both rest on His perfect character. God cannot lie. What He says is true and certain. The verse describes us as people "who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us." Picture someone running from danger to a place of safety and grabbing hold with both hands. That is what faith does. It runs to God's promises and holds on tight. On this quiet Saturday between the cross and the empty tomb, the disciples felt that their hope had died. But God's promises were still true. Today, whatever is uncertain, hold fast to what cannot change. God's Word is your strong consolation and sure refuge.
question: What uncertainty can you anchor today in a God who cannot lie?
prayer: Lord, You cannot lie, and Your promises never change. When everything feels uncertain, I flee to You for refuge and hold fast to the hope set before me. Amen.

text: If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.
reflection: On this Easter Sunday, we celebrate a God who keeps His word. Paul writes, "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." The disciples had scattered, doubted, and even denied Jesus. Yet on the third day, He rose, exactly as He had promised. Their faith had faltered, but His faithfulness did not. That is the hope of Easter. The empty tomb is proof that God's promises stand, even when our faith is weak. Jesus did not stay in the grave because He cannot deny Himself. He is the resurrection and the life, and His word always comes true. Perhaps your faith feels small today. Perhaps you have doubted or wandered. The risen Christ still comes to you, just as He came to His frightened disciples. He remains faithful. Celebrate today not because your faith is strong, but because your Savior is. He is risen, and His faithfulness is forever.
question: Where has your faith faltered, and how does the risen Jesus answer it with His faithfulness?
prayer: Risen Lord, even when I believe not, You abide faithful. Thank You for keeping Your word and rising from the dead. Let my hope rest in You today. Amen.

text: She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.
reflection: Martha was grieving. Her brother Lazarus had died, and Jesus had arrived four days late. Yet when Jesus asked if she believed He was the resurrection and the life, she answered with one of the clearest confessions of faith in the Gospels: "Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world." She did not yet understand everything. She could not see how Jesus would bring good out of her loss. But she knew who He was. That is often how faith works. We do not always understand what God is doing, but we can know who He is. Faith rests on His identity, not our circumstances. Just after Easter, this verse reminds us that the risen Jesus is the One who meets us in our grief. If you are hurting today, bring your sorrow to Him. And like Martha, speak your faith even through tears.
question: What sorrow can you bring to Jesus today while still speaking your faith in Him?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the resurrection and the life. Meet me in my grief, and help me say, even through tears, that I believe You are the Christ, the Son of God. Amen.

text: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
reflection: Paul describes the place where every believer now stands: "By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God." Through Jesus, we have access into grace. Grace is not just a doorway we pass through once. It is the ground we stand on every day. We do not stand in God's favor because of our performance on good days, and we do not fall out of it on bad days. We stand in grace. And from that secure position, we rejoice in hope. We look forward to the glory of God, to the day when everything He has promised is fulfilled. This changes how we face each day. We are not trying to climb into God's favor. We are already standing in it. Today, plant your feet firmly in His grace. Let go of the fear of falling out of His love, and let hope fill you with joy.
question: How would it change today to remember that you already stand in God's grace?
prayer: Lord, through Jesus I have access to the grace in which I stand. Free me from the fear of falling out of Your love, and fill me with hope of Your glory. Amen.

text: Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.
reflection: In the middle of a difficult vision about evil and judgment, John pauses to highlight God's faithful people: "Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus." In a world full of pressure to compromise, these people endured. They kept obeying God and kept trusting Jesus. Their faith was not a quick burst of enthusiasm but a long, patient perseverance. That is a beautiful picture of living by faith. It is not always dramatic. Often it looks like ordinary faithfulness, day after day. Keeping God's commands when it would be easier to cut corners. Holding on to Jesus when others let go. Remaining patient when answers are slow. As March comes to a close, consider what living by faith has meant for you this month. Ask God for the patience of the saints. Keep trusting, keep obeying, and keep holding on to Jesus. Faithful endurance is never forgotten by Him.
question: Where is God asking you for patient endurance, to keep trusting and keep obeying?
prayer: Lord, give me the patience of the saints. Help me keep Your commandments and hold on to the faith of Jesus, through every pressure, to the end. Amen.
